hook.text: To a language model, berry is token nineteen seven seven two.

teeth.text: Two doors down, at nineteen seven seven oh, sits teeth. And cherry? Way off at sixty thousand two twenty-five.

label.text: By the numbers, berry's a lot more like teeth. Which is nonsense. IDs are just labels.

vector.text: [slowly] So the model swaps each ID for a vector: a list of a few thousand numbers.

embedding.text: [slowly] That list is the token's embedding: its row in a table learned in training.

geometry.text: And lists of numbers have geometry. They can sit close together, or far apart.

toy.text: Here's the lesson's tiny version, with three numbers per word.

nearest.text: Measure from cat. Kitten's nearest, then dog. Wolf's further out, and truck's way over there.

learned.text: Nobody wrote that down. Training pushes words that turn up in similar sentences toward similar vectors.

generalize.text: So once a model's seen the cat sat on the mat, the dog sat on the mat is half handled already.

axes.text: One catch. We named these three dimensions so we could read them. Real ones have no names.

nameless.text: Dimension eighteen forty-seven of a real model doesn't mean anything you could point to. The meaning's in the whole arrangement.

order.text: And embeddings on their own can't see order.

bites.text: Dog bites man, and man bites dog, are the same three vectors, shuffled.

set.text: Treat them as a bag of vectors, and the two sentences are identical.

position.text: So the model mixes in where each token sits. Dog in the first slot gets a different vector from dog in the last.

order-in.text: Now, if meaning is closeness, how do you measure close?

ruler.text: The obvious tool is a ruler. Straight-line distance.

length.text: But a ruler also counts how long each vector is. And in an embedding, length mostly tracks how common a word is, not what it means.

cosine.text: So we measure the angle instead. That's cosine similarity.

same.text: These two point the same way, and one's five times longer. The ruler says five point seven apart. Cosine says one. A perfect match.

right.text: At a right angle, cosine is zero. Unrelated. Pointing opposite ways, it's minus one.

search.text: That's enough for a working search.

query.text: Now ask, how did the company perform financially?

hit.text: Top hit, earnings beat analyst expectations, at point nine nine eight. Not one word in common with the question.

meaning.text: The search runs on meaning, not on text.

blind.text: It does have blind spots. The drug is effective, and the drug is not effective, land almost on top of each other.

rerank.text: Close isn't true, and it isn't always useful. So real systems add a second pass that actually reads the top hits.

sim-in.text: And one vector per word has a bigger problem. Some words mean nothing until you see their neighbours.

trophy.text: The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because it was too big. What was too big? The trophy.

small.text: Make it too small, and now it's the suitcase.

pronoun.text: The pronoun never changed. Its meaning comes from the words around it.

attention.text: Attention is how each token pulls in information from the others, weighted by how relevant each one is.

query-vec.text: To do that, every token turns its embedding into three vectors. A query: what am I looking for?

key.text: A key: what do I offer?

value.text: And a value: what I hand over when I'm picked.

scores.text: The pronoun's query is compared with every key, for one score each.

weights.text: Point four six of the pronoun's attention goes to trophy.

real.text: Here's the actual arithmetic, on two-number vectors.

dot.text: Multiply them number by number and add it up: that's a dot product. It's cosine similarity, without dividing by the lengths.

blend.text: The pronoun's new vector is that blend of the values, pulled toward trophy's.

flip.text: Point the query at suitcase instead, and the blend follows. A different question gets a different answer.

heads.text: A real model runs many of these side by side, called heads, each with its own idea of relevant. And it stacks them dozens of layers deep.

square.text: Each token scores itself and every token before it, never a later one.

attn-in.text: So let's put all the pieces in order.

path.text: Your text becomes token IDs. Each ID becomes its embedding, plus its position.

block.text: Then comes a block. Attention mixes information between tokens, then a feed-forward network works on each token alone.

residual.text: Around each half, the input's added back in, so nothing gets lost.

repeat.text: And the block repeats. Thirty-two times, in the lesson's mid-sized model.

params.text: That model has about seven billion parameters. So where do they live?

split.text: The embedding table holds half a billion, and the output layer, which scores every token, as much again.

ff.text: The feed-forward networks hold three point eight billion. Fifty-four percent of the whole model.

knowledge.text: That's where much of what it knows lives. There's no fact database in there. Just weights.

wide.text: Width sets how much one token's vector can hold. Depth sets how many times it gets refined. You need both.

experts.text: The biggest open models split that feed-forward half into many experts, and run only a few for each token.

deepseek.text: DeepSeek V3 stores six hundred seventy-one billion parameters, and each token uses thirty-seven billion of them.

top.text: And at the very top, the last token's vector becomes one score for every token in the vocabulary. A hundred and twenty-eight thousand scores.

next.text: Something still has to pick one.

docs.text: Five tiny documents, hand-scored on four themes, standing in for real embeddings.

softmax.text: Softmax turns the scores into weights that add up to one.

ten.text: Ten tokens make fifty-five scores. Double the text to twenty, and it's two hundred and ten, nearly four times the work.

scale.text: Then it's divided by the square root of two, since each vector has two numbers. That keeps the scores small.
